evidence.description: The task promotes its weak reference to a strong self before entering the repeating loop and uses that reference throughout the loop.
The task is stored on the instance, and its only explicit cancellation occurs in deinit.

candidates.explanation: Although the task captures self weakly, the guard creates a strong reference that remains alive throughout the loop. The instance owns the task, and the running task retains the instance. Consequently, releasing other references cannot trigger the deinitializer that is supposed to cancel the task.
candidates.title: Long-running task retains its owner

evidence.description: The initial interval is fetched and assigned but never used.
The loop fetches a separate interval for sleeping rather than using initialInterval.

candidates.explanation: The initialInterval binding is unused. Its initializer still performs an awaited actor-property read before the first publication, adding unnecessary work and a suspension opportunity without contributing to the calculation or timer interval.
candidates.title: Unused initial interval fetch

evidence.description: The interval is multiplied and converted directly to UInt64 without validating its sign, finiteness, or representable range.
The count calculation divides by timePerTree and converts the floating-point result directly to Int without validation.

candidates.explanation: Both floating-point-to-integer conversions can trap for non-finite or out-of-range values; the UInt64 conversion also cannot represent negative results. A zero timePerTree can produce a non-finite count calculation. No validation is visible before either conversion, and try? only handles errors thrown by Task.sleep, not traps while evaluating its argument.
candidates.title: Unchecked numeric conversions can trap
